pullman-illinois.story:
Pullman was a company town founded in the 1880s just outside the Chicago city limits by George Pullman's railway car company. About 6,000 employees and as many dependants lived there, in company housing with company markets, a library, churches and entertainment. At their height, more than 2,500 company towns housed about 3 percent of Americans.

During the Panic of 1893 the company cut wages and hours while leaving rents and store prices where they were. That led to the Pullman Strike of 1894. A national commission called the company's paternalism un-American and blamed it partly for the strike. The town had already become part of Chicago in 1889, when Hyde Park Township, which included Pullman, was annexed by a popular vote that most Pullman residents opposed. Annexation did not end the company's ownership. In 1898 the Supreme Court of Illinois ordered the company to sell all property not used for industry, and the company did not fully comply until 1907.

Pullman differs from a special district because the company ruled through ownership and contracts and never held a public charter to govern. It shows that a state court can order a corporation out of the business of owning a town, and that a neighbouring city can absorb such a town by a vote of the wider township while the company still owns the houses. Later American towns of this type declined from the 1920s, and later law, such as Marsh v. Alabama in 1946, kept constitutional rights in force on company streets that remained.
pullman-illinois.why: Annexation to Chicago was in 1889 by public vote, before the 1898 ruling, not after it; added that the company did not fully comply until 1907.

add_sources.t: The History of Pullman, Historic Pullman Foundation

wrangel-island-expedition.story:
Wrangel Island lies in the Arctic Ocean north of Siberia, across the Chukchi Sea from Alaska, and in 1921 nobody lived on it. It had already killed people. In 1914 survivors of the ship Karluk, crushed in the ice during an expedition organised by the Arctic explorer Vilhjalmur Stefansson, were stranded there for nine months until their captain walked across the sea to Siberia for help.

Stefansson believed the island could be claimed by simply occupying it. Russia had declared it Russian in 1916, but in 1921 he sent five people on a speculative attempt to claim it for Canada, saying he wanted to head off a Japanese claim. They were the Canadian Allan Crawford and the Americans Fred Maurer, Lorne Knight and Milton Galle, and Ada Blackjack, an Iñupiaq woman of about 23 from Nome, Alaska. She had been abandoned by her husband, cleaned houses and sewed for miners, and could not afford to care for her son. She took the job as seamstress and cook, sewing the fur clothing, in order to earn money for him.

A relief ship, the Teddy Bear, stuck in the ice in 1922 and turned back. Food ran short. In January 1923 Crawford, Maurer and Galle set out across the frozen sea toward Siberia to get help and were never seen again. Knight, too sick to go, died of scurvy that June. Blackjack nursed him and then, alone, kept herself alive for nearly two more months, until Harold Noice arrived by ship to rescue her on 19 August 1923. By then she had been on the island for about 23 months.

The same ship left a new party of 13, the American Charles Wells and 12 Inuit. In 1924 the Soviet Union sent the ship Krasny Oktyabr, or Red October, and took them away, by then 14 people after a birth on the island. Wells died of pneumonia in Vladivostok, two children died, and the survivors got home with money raised by the American Red Cross.

The island remains Russian and became a World Heritage Site in 2004. The episode shows the two ways a small private colony fails. The first is supply, because a single missed ship can mean death. The second is that an occupation without a government's backing has no protection, since the nearest state can end it by sending one vessel.
wrangel-island-expedition.why: 'Eight months' does not match the dates: the men left 28 January, Knight died 23 June, rescue 19 August 1923. Stated dates instead.

pegasus-air-launch.story:
Pegasus was a small rocket dropped from an aircraft. Orbital Sciences began developing it in 1987 with Hercules Aerospace and without government money for the development, and it has been described as the first privately developed orbital launch vehicle. The first flight, on 5 April 1990, used a NASA B-52. By 1994 the company had moved to Stargazer, a converted Lockheed L-1011 airliner formerly owned by Air Canada.

The aircraft released the rocket at about 12,000 metres over open ocean, where it fell for five seconds before its first stage lit. The aircraft took off from places including Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral in Florida, Vandenberg and Dryden in California, Wallops in Virginia, Kwajalein in the Pacific, and the Canary Islands in the Atlantic. There have been 46 launches. The 46th, on 3 July 2026 Eastern time from Kwajalein, was the first since 2021 and carried Katalyst Space's LINK spacecraft, sent to raise the orbit of NASA's Swift observatory. LINK reached orbit but could not control its orientation, and on 19 August 2026 Katalyst and NASA concluded that the reboost was not possible.

The rocket matters here because at the moment of release nothing is below it except open sea, and the launch site is an aircraft. The Outer Space Treaty speaks of a state's "territory or facility", and no court has had to say what that means for an air launch. The legal writer Marco Pedrazzi suggests two readings. A registered aircraft could be considered a facility of the state of registry, or the state from which the aircraft took off could be treated as the state from which the launch took place.

These questions did not come up because the company was American, its launches were licensed, and no damage claim is known. Pegasus shows that the technique works. It shows nothing about doing it without a state.
pegasus-air-launch.why: Confirmed 46th launch; added what the July 2026 flight carried and how it ended.

add_sources.t: Mission to Rescue NASA Swift Observatory Launches, Via Satellite
No-Go for Katalyst's Reboost of NASA's Swift Observatory, SpacePolicyOnline
Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, Marco Pedrazzi

liberty-reserve.story:
Liberty Reserve was a private digital currency service in San José, Costa Rica. It billed itself as a payment system for people without bank accounts, and it had over one million users when it was shut. Users could register and move money with only a name, an email address and a birth date, and the site made no effort to verify identities.

Its founder had a prior record in this business. Arthur Budovsky and a partner had run a digital currency exchange called Gold Age from 2002 to 2006 and were indicted in New York in 2006 for operating an illegal financial business. Budovsky moved to Costa Rica and incorporated Liberty Reserve in 2006. Costa Rican authorities told it in 2009 that it needed a licence as a money transmitter, and in 2011 they denied it a business licence over a lack of transparency about its funding. The company formally disbanded at that point in Costa Rica, and Budovsky kept operating.

In May 2013 US federal prosecutors shut it down under the Patriot Act after an investigation across 17 countries. They charged Budovsky and six others with money laundering and with running an unlicensed financial business, and they alleged more than $6 billion in criminal proceeds had passed through. Spanish police arrested Budovsky at Madrid's Barajas airport that month. The chief technology officer, Mark Marmilev, pleaded guilty and received five years in December 2014. Budovsky pleaded guilty in January 2016 to conspiring to commit money laundering, and on 6 May 2016 he was sentenced to 20 years in prison.

The case combines a private currency with an offshore base and a host that did not act decisively. The project still lost, because its links to the dollar and to customers ran through places the United States could reach, and because other governments cooperated.
liberty-reserve.why: Added how the case ended: Budovsky's 2016 plea and 20-year sentence.

smyrtos-interdiction-2026.story:
On 14 June 2026 Royal Marine Commandos and specialist officers boarded the oil tanker Smyrtos in the English Channel. She was carrying more than 100,000 tonnes of Russian crude and flying the flag of Cameroon, which had expelled her from its register that May. Her Indian captain, Ajay Pant, was arrested and charged under Britain's Russia sanctions regulations with controlling a ship delivering prohibited oil from Russia to a third country, an offence with a maximum of ten years in prison. It was described as Britain's first solo interdiction of a sanctioned tanker.

Britain relied on Article 110 of UNCLOS and on its own law, and its Ministry of Defence said that "where a vessel is determined stateless, the UK can exercise powers available under its domestic legislation". Accounts of the location changed. Early government statements said the boarding took place on the high seas. Later ones said the ship had entered British waters, and the prosecutor said it had entered British territorial waters "without a legitimate flag".

That matters, because a country has full authority inside its own territorial sea and a much weaker claim outside it. The case belongs to a wider run of actions against the so-called shadow fleet, tankers that use opaque ownership and false flags. The United States seized the Marinera, formerly Bella 1, with British support and rejected her claimed Russian registration. It also boarded the M Sophia after she allegedly claimed Panamanian registry falsely.

In June 2025 a group of Nordic and Baltic states said vessels without a valid flag have no right to freedom of navigation. Thea Coventry of Leiden University argues that if the boarding took place on the high seas, Britain would need a basis such as universal jurisdiction, and that oil deliveries fall outside its accepted scope. She also suggests that repeated acts of this kind could shape a future customary rule if other states stay silent. A court denied the captain bail on 16 July 2026 and set his trial for 15 December 2026. The other 24 crew members were not charged.
smyrtos-interdiction-2026.why: Prosecution is pending, not of unknown result: bail denied 16 July 2026, trial set for 15 December 2026.

add_sources.t: UK Denies Bail to Captain of Detained Shadow Fleet Tanker, Maritime Executive
UK Court Holds Captain of Shadow Fleet Tanker for Trial, Maritime Executive

dahabshiil-barclays.story:
Dahabshiil is the largest money-transfer company in the Horn of Africa, with 400 payout locations in the region and its chief executive's office in London. For Somaliland, which has run itself since 1991 with no recognition for most of that time, companies like this are the financial system. Officials there said in 2014 that remittances from abroad came to about $400 million a year, 25 to 40 percent of the economy.

These companies depend on a few ordinary banks in the West that are willing to hold their accounts. In May 2013 Barclays, one of the last major banks still doing so, decided to close the accounts of such operators. A record $1.9 billion fine that US authorities had imposed on HSBC over dealings with banks in Mexico and Saudi Arabia appears to have made the business look too risky for the profits. Dahabshiil went to court, and a British High Court injunction postponed the closure without cancelling it.

The article reporting this quoted Somaliland's planning minister as saying the president had written letters and appealed repeatedly, without result. An unrecognised government had little diplomatic weight with which to press its case. UN agencies, the World Bank and large aid charities also used Dahabshiil to pay their staff and partners, which shows how widely the channel was relied on.

In April 2014 Barclays and Dahabshiil announced that they had settled on mutually acceptable terms. A person familiar with the matter said no money changed hands. Dahabshiil received a transition period in which to end its relationship with Barclays and move to other banking arrangements, so the account closed after all, on a later timetable. The case shows that the deciding point for a place with no recognition may be a compliance officer's review in London, far from any ministry.
dahabshiil-barclays.why: The outcome is known: April 2014 settlement with a transition period to leave Barclays.

add_sources.t: Barclays settles dispute with money transfer company Dahabshiil, Max Colchester, via Hiiraan Online

jam-v-ifc.story:
The International Finance Corporation is a World Bank institution based in Washington. It lent money to Coastal Gujarat Power Limited to build a coal-fired power plant in Gujarat, India. People living nearby, led by Budha Ismail Jam, sued it in the United States and said pollution from the plant harmed their air, land and water. The lower courts held that it was immune.

The question was what a 1945 American law meant by saying international organisations have the same immunity as foreign governments. In 1945 foreign governments had nearly total immunity. Since 1952 and a 1976 law they have had a narrower immunity, which leaves them open to suit over commercial activity. On 27 February 2019 the Supreme Court ruled by seven votes to one that the law means today's immunity, so that organisations and foreign governments stay on the same footing. Justice Breyer dissented.

The Corporation warned that this would expose development banks to lawsuits over their main work. The Court called that concern inflated. It noted that the law only provides default rules and that an organisation's charter can say something different. It did not decide whether this particular suit could go forward under the commercial activity rule, and sent the case back. On 14 February 2020 the federal district court in Washington, through Judge Bates, again found the Corporation immune. The commercial activity exception requires a suit to be based on conduct in the United States, and the court found that the heart of the complaint was the failure to ensure that the plant was built and run with due care in India, even though the loan was approved in Washington. It therefore never had to decide whether the lending was commercial. The plaintiffs appealed to the federal appeals court in Washington in 2021.

The case matters for anyone taking headquarters immunity as a model. Immunity comes from a statute or a charter and can shift with the law, and a body that does business may have much less of it than its founding documents suggest. The villagers' own suit shows the other side of that, since they won the point of law in the Supreme Court and then lost in the district court over where the conduct at the heart of their complaint took place.
jam-v-ifc.why: Added the 2020 remand decision: the IFC stayed immune because the suit's core conduct was in India.

add_sources.t: Jam v IFC before the D.C. District Court, EJIL: Talk!
Jam plaintiffs' appeal brief, February 2021, EarthRights

tornado-cash-sanctions.story:
Tornado Cash is software on the Ethereum blockchain that mixes crypto transfers so that it is hard to trace who sent what to whom. In August 2022 the US Treasury placed it on the sanctions list, making it illegal for US citizens, residents and companies to use it. Its domain and code accounts were shut.

On 26 November 2024 the Fifth Circuit appeals court ruled that its immutable smart contracts, programs no one can change, do not count as property under federal law, and that the Office of Foreign Assets Control lacked authority to sanction the software directly, as opposed to the people and groups who abuse it. On 21 March 2025 the Treasury lifted the sanctions and said it remained concerned about North Korean hacking and laundering.

People fared differently from code. Alexey Pertsev was arrested in Amsterdam on 10 August 2022 and sentenced by a Dutch court on 14 May 2024 to 5 years and 4 months. Roman Storm and Roman Semenov were charged in the United States in August 2023 with assisting in laundering about $1 billion. After a three-week trial in 2025, a jury in August found Storm guilty of conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business, which carries up to five years in prison, and could not agree on the money laundering and sanctions charges. Prosecutors chose to try those again. Storm asked the judge to acquit him on all three charges, and as of August 2026 that motion was undecided. Judge Katherine Polk Failla moved the retrial from October 2026 to 26 April 2027.

For a project thinking of a crypto treasury, this is the nearest thing to a court test. Software nobody controls proved hard to sanction under one statute in one court. The writers and operators remained open to criminal charges in two countries. How the question would go under other statutes or other countries' laws is not settled.
tornado-cash-sanctions.why: Added the hung counts, the pending acquittal motion and the retrial date of April 2027.

add_sources.t: Tornado Cash developer Roman Storm's retrial delayed to April 2027, Cointelegraph

micula-romania.story:
The Micula case began with a tax break. With effect from 1 April 1999, Romania adopted an investment incentive scheme for certain regions, known as EGO 24. In the early 2000s the claimants built a large, integrated food production business in the region, relying on the scheme. In 2002 Romania and Sweden signed a treaty protecting each other's investors and allowing arbitration at ICSID.

Then Romania began joining the European Union, which it did on 1 January 2007. The EU told it that schemes like EGO 24 broke the rules against state aid, meaning government subsidies that distort competition. Romania repealed nearly all the incentives. On 28 July 2005 the claimants asked for arbitration. On 11 December 2013 the tribunal ruled that Romania had breached the treaty and awarded about £70 million plus interest, and Romania's attempt to annul the award failed.

Romania's partial payment led to a clash between two legal systems. On 26 May 2014 the European Commission ordered it to stop, and on 30 March 2015 it decided that paying the award would be illegal state aid. The European General Court annulled that decision on 18 June 2019 because the Commission had applied its powers to events before Romania joined. On 19 February 2020 the United Kingdom Supreme Court unanimously lifted a stay so that the award could be enforced there. The Commission appealed, and in January 2022 the EU Court of Justice set aside the General Court's ruling. It held that the right to compensation arose only with the award of 2013, after Romania had joined, so the Commission had power over it, and that under its Achmea judgment the arbitration clause between two member states had been displaced by EU law when Romania joined. On 2 October 2024 the General Court, deciding the case again, upheld the Commission's view that the award is state aid, treating the Micula brothers and their companies as one economic unit so that partial payments could be recovered from any of them. That decision could still be appealed. In March 2024 the Court of Justice also dealt with infringement proceedings against the United Kingdom for allowing the award to be enforced there.

The case shows that a repealed incentive can cost a state money under a treaty, and that collecting takes many years and may be blocked by another legal order, so that a court in one system enforces what a court in another treats as unlawful.
micula-romania.why: The story stopped at the Commission's appeal; added the January 2022 Court of Justice reversal and the October 2024 General Court ruling from the listed blog.

darwin-port-landbridge.story:
The Port of Darwin is in Australia's Northern Territory. In late 2014 and early 2015 the territory's government invited offers, and 33 companies signalled interest. In October 2015 Landbridge, privately held and based in Rizhao, China, won a 99-year lease for A$506 million, more than 25 times the port's profit over the previous two years, and promised to invest A$200 million over 25 years. Its owner, the billionaire Ye Cheng, has close ties to the Chinese Communist Party, and the port lies near a base used by United States Marines and an airport with military use.

A senior defence official raised concerns in 2015. A review in 2021 found no national security grounds to overturn the lease, and in October 2023 the federal government said it would not cancel it. In April 2025 Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Australia sought to buy back the port, and both main parties promised during the election campaign to return it to Australian ownership. The former chief minister, Adam Giles, defended his decision. China's ambassador criticised the plan, and in January 2026 warned that nationalising the port would harm trade and relations.

On 24 April 2026 Landbridge filed a claim at the World Bank's arbitration centre, ICSID, under the free trade agreement between Australia and China, saying that Australia's actions were discriminatory. Transport Minister Catherine King said the government was disappointed and would defend the claim while talks continued, and she called control of the port a national security issue. Experts quoted in the trade press said arbitration could take years, and how it will end is not known.

The case shows that a territory's government can grant a long lease, that security arguments can return ten years later, and that the operator's remaining protection may lie in a treaty claim.
darwin-port-landbridge.why: Exact filing date, forum and treaty added; government response added.

add_sources.t: Chinese firm files arbitration over Australia's move to reclaim Darwin port, Maritime Executive

panama-ports-hutchison.story:
Panama Ports Company, a subsidiary of Hong Kong's CK Hutchison, has run the container ports of Balboa on the Pacific side of the Panama Canal and Cristóbal on the Atlantic side since the 1990s. Its contract renewed automatically in 2021 for another 25 years. The canal carries an estimated 5 percent of world maritime trade, and the United States handed the canal itself to Panama in 1999.

At the start of 2025 President Donald Trump threatened to take control of the canal, saying it was in effect under Chinese control. CK Hutchison announced that it would sell dozens of ports, including these two, to a group led by BlackRock for nearly $23 billion, and the deal appeared to stall after objections from China. A lawsuit filed in 2025 said that the contracts rested on unconstitutional laws. An audit reported accounting errors said to have cost Panama about $300 million since the extension.

On the evening of 29 January 2026 Panama's Supreme Court announced that the laws and acts underpinning the contracts were unconstitutional. The company denied all the allegations and said the ruling lacked legal basis. China said it would take necessary measures to protect its companies. In February 2026 Panama ordered the two ports occupied and gave temporary contracts to a Maersk subsidiary, APM Terminals, for Balboa and an MSC subsidiary, TiL, for Cristóbal, with a new long-term concession process expected to finish in the last quarter of 2026. The company brought an arbitration claim at the International Chamber of Commerce and expanded it, reporting losses above $2 billion. In April 2026 it also began arbitration in London against Maersk, alleging that Maersk had broken a long-term contract by siding with the government.

The case shows that a court can end a port concession of nearly 30 years in one judgment, and that the operator then turns to arbitration for money.
panama-ports-hutchison.why: Replaced headline reporting with what happened after the ruling: interim operators, ICC claim, London claim against Maersk.

add_sources.t: Panama's port crisis, Container Magazine
CK Hutchison's Panama Unit Files Arbitration Against Maersk, Maritime Professional

un-sea-level-declaration-2026.story:
On 24 September 2026 the UN General Assembly adopted a political declaration on sea-level rise by consensus of all 193 member states. It affirms a presumption in favour of continued statehood despite sea-level rise, along with sovereignty, sovereign rights and responsibilities, and UN membership. It also says that once baselines have been established under the Law of the Sea treaty, states may keep their maritime zones despite physical changes from rising seas.

The path to it ran through small island states. The Pacific Islands Forum issued declarations on maritime zones in 2021 and on statehood in 2023, arguing that a state continues to exist even if its territory is fully inundated. The International Law Commission backed that view in 2025, and the General Assembly recognised its contribution without endorsing its conclusions. A General Assembly resolution affirming continuity, 80/263, passed in May 2026 with 141 votes in favour, eight states against and 28 abstaining, according to the accounts of the vote, including that of Harry Aitken, an Australian legal adviser who led the negotiations on the declaration's legal elements and was writing in a personal capacity.

In its 2025 climate opinion the International Court of Justice said losing territory "would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood". Judges Tomka and Aurescu wrote separately from opposite sides. Tomka called the Court's position a precocious leap of legal reasoning, given the silence of many states, and wrote that "territory has been indispensable to the concept of a State". Aurescu criticised the Court for saying nothing about keeping UN membership, a gap the declaration addresses. The declaration does not explain how the principles would work in practice. It speaks of relocation as something that may be needed, that must be voluntary and consistent with international law, and that it calls "mobility with dignity".

The only concrete step Aitken cites is the 2024 treaty between Australia and Tuvalu. For anyone interested in places outside existing countries, the point is that the requirement of territory has been loosened only for existing states. Nothing in the declaration helps a new body with no territory become a state. It also says nothing about artificial structures. Whether it becomes binding law will depend on how states act.
un-sea-level-declaration-2026.why: The resolution with 8 against and 28 abstaining is 80/263 of May 2026, not a 2025 resolution. Tomka and Aurescu criticised the Court from opposite sides, not jointly for ambiguity.

add_sources.t: Statehood and sea level rise, EJIL: Talk!

sea-rise-continuity-resolution.story:
No state has ever lost all its land to the sea, so the law had no direct answer to what would then happen to it. In recent years the answer has developed quickly. The Pacific Islands Forum declared in 2023 that the presumption of continuity of statehood applies in the context of climate-related sea-level rise.

In its climate advisory opinion of 23 July 2025, the International Court of Justice said at paragraph 363 that "once a State is established, the disappearance of one of its constituent elements would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood". Thirty-three states and seven organisations had addressed statehood in the case, although the question put to the Court did not mention it. Commentators read the sentence in two ways, as a restatement of the ordinary rule or as acceptance that a state can survive without territory. The Court did not mention sea level in that sentence. Judge Tomka questioned the basis for a wider reading in practice, and Vice-President Sebutinde and Judge Aurescu wanted it firmer.

The International Law Commission's study group treated continuity as the answer in a final report in 2025, saying its conclusions could become law if states adopt instruments. The General Assembly then adopted resolution 80/263 in May 2026, with 141 votes in favour, eight against and 28 abstentions. Quoting the Court, it said it "affirms the continuity of statehood in the face of sea level rise". Britain said it was intended to reflect the opinion and not to develop it. On 24 September 2026 all 193 member states agreed by consensus a political declaration affirming a presumption in favour of continued statehood, including UN membership.

The legal conditions and consequences of continuity remain open. A commenter asked where a submerged state's population would live and where its government would sit. None of this creates new states.
sea-rise-continuity-resolution.why: Added month and full vote for 80/263, and the later consensus declaration of September 2026.

add_sources.t: UN declaration on sea-level rise, Just Security

white-rajahs-sarawak.story:
Sarawak is a territory on the north-west coast of Borneo, today a state of Malaysia. For 105 years it was ruled by a British family, the Brookes, who held the title of Rajah, a word for a king or prince. It is one of the few cases on record of a private person from abroad gaining a territory and ruling it as a monarch.

Before 1841 Sarawak was part of the realm of the Sultanate of Brunei, and owed loyalty to the sultan. James Brooke, a man of British origin born in India in 1803, helped the sultan's side fight piracy and uprisings among the local peoples. The sultan's representative, Pengiran Muda Hashim, promised him Sarawak in return for that help and then delayed. On 24 September 1841, after Brooke called on him with an armed ship, Hashim granted him the area around the town of Sarawak, now Kuching, and the nearby Bau mining district. Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddin II confirmed the appointment by July 1842. No price was paid, and in 1846 the sultan recognised Brooke's authority without requiring tribute.

Brooke rebuilt the government on the British model. He and his successor leased or annexed more land from Brunei until the state covered much of northern Borneo. James's will set the succession along the male line. His nephew Charles ruled from 1868 to 1917, and Charles's son Vyner from 1917 to 1946. In 1941, just before the Japanese invasion in the Second World War, Vyner ended the Rajah's absolute rule by giving new powers to the Council Negri, the local parliament.

After the Japanese occupation, Vyner ceded Sarawak to Britain as a Crown colony on 1 July 1946, citing a lack of money for reconstruction. Cession means a formal handing-over of territory. It was contested from the start. His nephew and legal heir, Anthony Brooke, objected, and so did most native members of the Council Negri. Because it was unclear whether the cession was legal, Britain also passed an annexation bill. An anti-cession movement grew, and the British governor Duncan Stewart was assassinated by members of a group seeking union with Indonesia. Sarawak became a British Crown colony, and in 1963 it became a state of Malaysia under the Malaysia Agreement.

The family's grant shows what such a position rested on. Brooke's title came from a ruler who had the power to give it and who owed him a favour, in a place where no stronger outside power objected. Other states took different positions on what Sarawak was. The United States recognised it in 1850, and Britain appointed a consul and recognised it in 1864. The Netherlands refused. By a treaty of 14 June 1888 Sarawak became a state protected by Britain, governing itself at home while Britain ran its foreign relations and held a veto over any cession of its territory to a foreign state. The rule lasted as long as outside powers accepted it, and it ended when one family member signed it away over the objection of his heir and of the local parliament.
white-rajahs-sarawak.why: The text said foreign treatment of Sarawak was unknown; it is known (US 1850, UK 1864, Dutch refusal, 1888 protectorate). Also, the 1841 grant was made by Hashim under armed pressure and confirmed by the sultan by 1842.

add_sources.t: Raj of Sarawak, Wikipedia

t3-ice-island-escamilla.story:
T-3, also called Fletcher's Ice Island, was a huge slab of glacial ice in the Arctic Ocean, about 11 by 5 kilometres and roughly 99 percent ice. It moved slowly around the ocean with the currents. It was found during US Air Force reconnaissance flights over the Arctic that began in 1946, though the exact date is disputed, and from 1952 the US Air Force and Navy used it as a research platform, under Colonel Joseph O. Fletcher, because it was so steady. It had huts, a power plant and an airstrip, and it held a permanent station from October 1962, usually with 25 to 30 staff. The only authority on site was a station manager, chosen by the Naval Arctic Research Laboratory.

On 16 July 1970 an argument broke out over some home-made raisin wine. Mario Escamilla, the wine's owner, was told that a co-worker, Donald Leavitt, had taken it. Escamilla borrowed a rifle and went back to his trailer to confront him. The station manager, Bennie Lightsey, stopped him and tried to take the rifle, and in the struggle Lightsey was shot and killed. There were 19 people on the team then, and now they had a killing with no police or court, on a piece of ice that belonged to no one.

Both men were Americans, but that does not by itself let a US court try a crime abroad. Federal crimes need a legal hook, called jurisdiction, meaning a court's authority over a place or event. The ice then lay inside the Arctic sector Canada had claimed, but Canada chose not to act. American officials flew Escamilla to Dulles Airport in Virginia and charged him under the special law for crimes at sea, arguing that the ice was on the high seas, the open ocean outside every country's waters.

A jury convicted him of involuntary manslaughter and he received three years. In 1972 the Fourth Circuit, a federal appeals court, heard the case with six judges and split evenly on whether US law reached an unclaimed ice island. An even split leaves the trial court's ruling in place, so the case stayed in American courts without any rule being set. The judges did find other errors in the trial and ordered a new one, at which he was acquitted. Congress settled the question only in 1984, by adding 18 U.S.C. section 7(7), which covers offences by or against a US national at a place outside the jurisdiction of any nation.

The last station closed on 1 October 1974, the site was last visited in 1979, and the ice drifted on. The case shows what happens when something odd is neither land nor a ship. Living beyond clear national law did not remove anyone's government. It left people with no local police, and when something went wrong, the country that supplied the station stepped in and argued about the legal reasons afterwards.
t3-ice-island-escamilla.why: Listed Wikipedia source gives final closure on 1 October 1974 and last visit in 1979, not abandonment in 1978; 1947 first sighting is disputed there. Named the 1984 statute. Lightsey is spelled Bennie here and Benny on Wikipedia; left as is.

larsen-hawaiian-kingdom.story:
Larsen v. Hawaiian Kingdom was an arbitration administered by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague under the UNCITRAL rules, a standard set of arbitration procedures. It began on 8 November 1999 and ended with an award on 5 February 2001. Hawaii was an independent kingdom until the overthrow of its queen in 1893 and annexation by the United States in 1898, and many Hawaiians consider both illegal. Lance Paul Larsen, a resident of Hawaii, brought a case against the Hawaiian Kingdom, acting through what the case papers call its Council of Regency, whose representative was a man named Sai, and said that the kingdom had failed to protect him from the United States and the State of Hawaii. Since both agreed to arbitrate, the case could proceed.

The real goal, according to accounts of the case, was to have United States rule in Hawaii declared a breach of treaty obligations and of international law. The United States was not a party. The panel, made up of James Crawford as president, Gavan Griffith and Christopher Greenwood, applied the Monetary Gold principle, the rule that a tribunal cannot rule on the legal rights of an absent state that has not consented. It said that this left it with no dispute it could decide. In the panel's words, in the absence of the United States, the tribunal could neither decide that Hawaii is not part of the USA, nor proceed on the assumption that it is not, because to do either would disregard a principle going to the heart of the arbitral function in international law.

The case is sometimes quoted as though the Court had recognised the kingdom. The panel's words show otherwise, since it refused to assume anything on that question. The lesson is procedural. Two parties can agree to arbitrate almost anything, and the result binds only them. A state that stays out cannot be bound, and no ruling about its territory can result from a case it did not join.
larsen-hawaiian-kingdom.why: 'Around 2000' replaced with the 1999 start and 5 February 2001 award; the respondent was the Kingdom through its Council of Regency, not a man named Sai; added tribunal and the Monetary Gold rule.

add_sources.t: Larsen v. Hawaiian Kingdom, PCA Case 1999-01
Larsen note, American Journal of International Law

colorado-city-short-creek.story:
Colorado City, Arizona, founded as Short Creek in 1913, lies on the Utah line next to Hildale. It became home to a polygamist branch of Mormonism, the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints. A police raid in 1953 did not end the community. The town incorporated in September 1985, and most property was held by a church real estate trust called the United Effort Plan.

Under the leader Warren Jeffs, some 20 men were expelled in January 2004, and an estimated 400 young men were pushed out from 2001 to 2006. Jeffs was arrested on 28 August 2006. In 2007 state authorities began dismantling church ownership of the land. On 6 April 2010 county officials served search warrants on town officials over misuse of funds, and the Hildale public safety department was shut down.

On 21 June 2012 the United States Justice Department sued, alleging that Colorado City's government, including its police, was taking orders from the church. In July Arizona's attorney general funded daily sheriff's patrols. On 20 March 2014 a jury in a private suit, Cooke v. Colorado City, found that the towns had discriminated against a family because they were not members and awarded $5.2 million. On 7 March 2016 a federal jury in Phoenix found in the Justice Department's case that Colorado City, Hildale and their joint water company had discriminated on the basis of religion under the Fair Housing Act, and in an advisory verdict that the Colorado City Marshal's Office had acted as an arm of the church. A settlement that April paid $1,435,000 to nine people and $165,000 in civil penalties. On 18 April 2017 the court adopted the findings and ordered new police policies and hiring, two new officers, civil rights training, the subdivision of land in Colorado City, and a monitor to report on compliance. The town's population fell from 4,821 in 2010 to 2,478 in 2020.

This is the American example of a religious group holding both a town's land and its government for decades, and of the government eventually moving in through a land trust case, criminal charges and civil rights lawsuits.
colorado-city-short-creek.why: The suit was filed 21 June 2012, not July. Added its outcome: 2016 verdict, settlement, 2017 order and monitor.

add_sources.t: United States v. Town of Colorado City, US Department of Justice

comoros-bidoon-passports.story:
The Bidoon are stateless people living in Gulf countries, including the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait. Around a decade before 2018, the Comoros Islands, an Indian Ocean country, launched a programme with those two states to sell its citizenship to them, in return for cash to help develop the archipelago. The people receiving this nationality were being given papers by a country far from where they lived.

The first phase was meant to earn the Comoros $200 million in return for giving citizenship to 4,000 stateless families. After a short suspension the scheme went on in 2011 under a new agreement, which set the price of a passport at 4,600 euros and a minimum of 5,000 passports.

In 2018 a commission of the Comoros parliament reported that nearly 48,000 foreigners, mostly Bidoon, had received passports. It said thousands of passports had been sold outside official channels through what it called mafia networks, and that up to $100 million in revenue had gone missing, about 17 percent of a year's GDP. It said secret contracts, poor documentation and the number of groups of officials involved made it hard to find out how much was lost.

In November 2022 the State Security Court, whose rulings cannot be appealed, sentenced former president Ahmed Abdallah Sambi to life in prison for high treason over the sale of passports under a 2008 law. The prosecutor alleged that he had embezzled $1.8 billion, more than the country's GDP. His lawyer said no evidence showed the missing money, and Sambi, a rival of the sitting president, refused to attend the trial, saying it would not be fair.

This is the nearest real case to one state selling nationality in bulk to a whole group. It shows that paper nationality can be arranged by agreement among governments for people with no link to the country. How the holders have fared since is not known.
comoros-bidoon-passports.why: Added the 2022 life sentence of Sambi, the main legal outcome of the scandal.

add_sources.t: Ex-Comoros president given life sentence over passport scandal, Al Jazeera

cook-islands-niue-association.story:
The Cook Islands and Niue are Pacific places that run themselves in free association with New Zealand, the Cook Islands since 4 August 1965 and Niue since 19 October 1974. New Zealand cannot legislate for them. It acts on defence and foreign affairs only when their governments ask and with their consent. They manage their own immigration, and they have no citizenship of their own, since their people are New Zealand citizens. Their constitutions, a 1983 exchange of letters and a 2001 joint declaration describe the relationship.

They have gradually taken on the outward signs of a country. Both sign UN treaties and join UN bodies as states, the Cook Islands from 1992 and Niue from 1994. They are still not UN members. In 2025 Prime Minister Mark Brown of the Cook Islands said the UN had confirmed that his country did not meet membership requirements, and Foreign Minister Tingika Elikana said joining would need a referendum and a new look at the tie to New Zealand. He also spoke of a new constitutional agreement reflecting growing independence. A New Zealand foreign ministry spokesperson said that the Cook Islands is not a fully independent and sovereign state, and New Zealand has said that UN membership could cost its people automatic access to New Zealand citizenship.

The argument has also cost money. In February 2025 the Cook Islands signed several agreements with China, and the office of New Zealand's foreign minister, Winston Peters, treated this as a breach of trust. New Zealand paused NZ$18.2 million of funding that June and a further NZ$11.6 million that October, nearly NZ$30 million in all. In November 2025 Brown told his parliament that sovereignty was not up for negotiation, talks were continuing, and Niue had just reaffirmed its own relationship with New Zealand.

The status of these places is therefore argued by the governments concerned. They show that a small place can act internationally for decades without a seat at the UN, and that access to a larger partner's passport may be what holds it back from going further.
cook-islands-niue-association.why: Added the 2025 New Zealand funding pauses over the China agreements.

add_sources.t: Cook Islands PM outlines timeline of tensions with NZ, PMN

commission-v-malta-2025.story:
Malta ran a programme under which a foreigner could gain Maltese nationality, and with it citizenship of the European Union, through set payments and investments. The law behind it was the Maltese Citizenship Act as amended in 2020, with regulations on citizenship for exceptional services. EU citizenship matters because it gives the right to live and work in every member state, and each state must accept the others' grants of nationality. So one country's sale affects all the rest.

The European Commission took Malta to the Court of Justice of the European Union. Malta replied that nationality is decided by each member state's national law, that the treaties do not require a prior genuine link, and that no such duty can be drawn from international law or from the Nottebohm case.

On 29 April 2025 the Grand Chamber ruled against Malta. It said that a state manifestly disregards the special relationship of solidarity and good faith with its nationals when it sets up a naturalisation scheme based on a transaction. The Court said a programme of that sort amounts to the commercialisation of the status of national and, by extension, of Union citizenship. It noted that set payments occupied a key place in the scheme. It declared that Malta had failed to meet its obligations under Article 20 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU and Article 4(3) of the Treaty on European Union, and ordered Malta to pay costs.

Malta then announced that it would scrap the scheme and widen citizenship for exceptional services, and in July 2025 it moved to what it describes as a merit-based model. The ruling binds EU member states. It does not apply to programmes elsewhere in the world, whose passports depend on separate visa agreements.
commission-v-malta-2025.why: Added Malta's response. Rests on search-result headlines only, the detail page was not retrievable; caller may want to verify.

add_sources.t: Malta to scrap golden passport scheme, MaltaToday
Malta cuts transactional citizenship programme after ECJ ruling, Malta Invest

polish-government-in-exile.story:
When Germany occupied Poland in 1939, a Polish government formed abroad. It was based in turn in Paris from 1939, at Angers until June 1940, and in London from 1940 after the fall of France. It opposed German-occupied Poland during the war and then the Soviet-backed People's Republic of Poland after it.

The government in exile went on for about 51 years, far longer than the war that created it. For most of that time it lacked recognition from the major powers. France withdrew recognition on 29 June 1945, and the United States and Britain on 5 July 1945. The last was the Holy See, on 19 October 1972. The government remained in existence without effective power. On 22 December 1990, at the Royal Castle in Warsaw, its last president, Ryszard Kaczorowski, handed the state symbols, including the presidential banner, the seals and the original 1935 Constitution, to Lech Wałęsa, Poland's newly elected president. The winding-up of its London offices was declared complete on 31 December 1991. A government in exile is a political group that claims to be the rightful government of a state, cannot exercise power there and sits in another country, and it usually hopes to return one day. This one did see the system it opposed collapse.

Three features matter for anyone studying this form. It began as the government of an existing, recognised state, which gave its claim a legal basis that a brand new group would lack. It relied throughout on hosts, first France and then Britain, and Britain kept hosting it for 45 years after ceasing to recognise it. And its value lay in keeping a claim alive until conditions changed, while it held no land and governed no one at home. A community with no earlier state could copy the offices, the elections and the long patience, and it could not copy the original claim.
polish-government-in-exile.why: 'Around 1990' replaced with the 22 December 1990 handover. Added the 1945 loss of recognition, which the story omitted and which matters to its argument.

add_sources.t: Polish government-in-exile, Wikipedia

palestine-observer-state.story:
The United Nations lists two non-member states with a standing invitation to take part as observers in the General Assembly and to keep permanent observer missions at its headquarters. They are the Holy See and the State of Palestine. Palestine's status comes from General Assembly resolution 67/19 of 29 November 2012, which accorded it non-member observer state status by 138 votes to 9, with 41 abstentions.

This is a case of a body gaining the word "state" at the UN through a vote of existing members, without full membership, which requires a Security Council recommendation. For the purposes of this subject it shows three things. The status can be voted by a majority of states. A people's claim, its history and wide diplomatic support are what carried that vote. And the status did not settle the disputes on the ground, since control of the territory is a separate question. Governments differ on what the resolution means for statehood, and each decides recognition for itself. By September 2025, when Britain, Canada and France joined them, 157 of the 193 UN members recognised the State of Palestine. On 10 May 2024 the General Assembly voted by 143 to 9, with 25 abstentions, to give its mission a seat among member states in alphabetical order and new rights to submit proposals and speak for groups, and urged the Security Council to consider full membership favourably. Palestine still cannot vote in the Assembly or stand for election to UN organs.

A new project should not read this as a route open to anyone. The status went to a people with a long-standing claim to self-determination and many supportive governments. Taking it as a model would require those same things, and a private founder has none of them. The case belongs here because it marks the upper limit of what a seat near the table can give without membership.
palestine-observer-state.why: Story stopped at 2012. Added the vote, the May 2024 upgrade and the September 2025 recognition count.

add_sources.t: Resolution ES-10/23, Wikipedia
Recognition of Palestine, Wikiwand

chickasaw-marsh.story:
Chickasaw was a suburb of Mobile, Alabama, owned by the Gulf Shipbuilding Corporation. It had houses, streets, sewers, a business block and a post office, and to anyone walking through it looked like any other American town. Marsh, a Jehovah's Witness, stood on the sidewalk near the post office handing out religious literature. The company had posted notices banning such activity without permission. She was told to stop, refused, and was convicted under an Alabama trespass law.

In 1946 the United States Supreme Court reversed the conviction. Alabama argued that the company's rights over its town were the same as a homeowner's rights over guests, and the Court rejected that. It wrote that ownership does not always mean absolute dominion, and that the more an owner opens property for use by the public, the more the owner's rights are limited by the rights of those who use it. People in a company town, it reasoned, have the same need as other citizens to receive information and make decisions.

This is the leading American rule on how far a private town owner's power goes. Anyone planning a private town in the United States meets it first, because a town that functions as a town takes on some of the duties of government. The case limits what a private owner may do inside its land, and later rulings have kept it close to its facts. In 1968 the Court extended it to a shopping centre in Logan Valley. In Lloyd v. Tanner in 1972 it refused to go further, because a company town's owner performs the full spectrum of municipal powers and a shop owner does not. In Hudgens v. NLRB in 1976 it rejected the idea that large shopping centres are the functional equivalent of a town, which effectively abandoned Logan Valley. In Manhattan Community Access v. Halleck in 2019 it said the test is whether a private body exercises a power traditionally and exclusively held by the state. So a private developer would come under Marsh if it runs a whole town, and would stay outside it if it only opens private land to the public.
chickasaw-marsh.why: The text said later private spaces were an open question. The Supreme Court answered it in Lloyd, Hudgens and Halleck.

add_sources.t: State Action Doctrine and Free Speech, Constitution Annotated

launching-state-resolution.story:
The Liability Convention of 1972 and the Registration Convention of 1975 use the words "launching State" for a country that launches or procures a launch, or from whose territory or facility an object is launched. By the 1990s these words raised new problems. Private companies were buying launches across borders, and Sea Launch was firing rockets from a Liberian-registered rig on the open ocean. The UN's space committee took up a review of the concept.

The results were two General Assembly resolutions. Resolution 59/115, adopted on 10 December 2004, recommends that countries consider national laws to authorise and supervise non-governmental space activities, consider agreements on joint launches, and share their practice on transferring ownership of objects in orbit. It says plainly that nothing in it is an authoritative interpretation of, or a proposed amendment to, the two treaties. Resolution 62/101, adopted in 2007, is about registration practice.

It recommends that the state of the launch territory, where no prior agreement exists, contact those that could qualify as launching states so that they can jointly decide who registers, that launch providers advise owners to approach the proper states, and that after a change of supervision in orbit the state of registry report the new owner, orbit and function. It adds that if there is no state of registry, the appropriate state under Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty could send in that information.

General Assembly resolutions of this type are recommendations. So the words "territory or facility" remain undefined, and these texts cannot settle whether a flagged or unflagged platform is a facility. Legal writers fill the gap with argument. Marco Pedrazzi, for one, writes that a ship or aircraft could be considered a facility belonging to the state where it is registered, a reading that gives no answer for a platform with no flag. They do show that governments know of the gaps and chose to answer them with national laws and agreements, leaving the treaties unchanged.
launching-state-resolution.why: Added a scholarly view on what 'facility' means. Resolution texts themselves were not refetched.

add_sources.t: Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, Marco Pedrazzi

arktika-2007-flag.story:
The seabed under the North Pole is at the centre of a legal question about who may one day have rights to what lies under the Arctic Ocean. Under the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, a coastal state controls the resources in a zone reaching 200 nautical miles (about 370 km) from its shore, and it can seek rights over seabed beyond that if it shows by scientific evidence that the seabed is a natural extension of its land. Lindsay Parson of Britain's National Oceanography Centre explained that the 200-mile zones of the five Arctic coastal states leave a central area of about 300,000 to 400,000 square kilometres in question. Russia first submitted its claim to part of that seabed in 2001. As Arctic ice shrinks, the area has become easier to reach.

Arktika 2007 was the expedition that went to gather evidence. The research ship Akademik Fedorov left Saint Petersburg on 10 July 2007 with about 100 scientists and two small Mir submarines, and the nuclear icebreaker Rossiya led it through the ice. The scientists wanted to find out whether undersea ridges such as the Lomonosov Ridge are linked to the Siberian shelf. Early in the trip the Fedorov's propeller motor failed in the Barents Sea, and the crew fixed it within hours while the icebreaker turned back to help. After test dives north of Franz Josef Land, the expedition reached the Pole.

In August the two submarines went down to the seabed, a depth of 4,261 metres. This was the first crewed descent to the ocean floor at the Pole. Artur Chilingarov, the expedition's leader and a member of parliament, was on board along with the pilots Anatoly Sagalevich and Yevgeny Chernyaev. They collected specimens and left a rust-proof titanium flag. Chilingarov said people could find it in a thousand years. All three were later named Heroes of the Russian Federation.

Other governments answered quickly. Canada's foreign minister, Peter MacKay, said this was not the 15th century, when countries could plant flags and claim territory. A US State Department spokesman said the flag had no legal standing. Parson called the dive a scientific achievement that meant very little as a legal claim.

The legal reason is the one that matters to anyone hoping to claim part of the world by arriving first. Under the Law of the Sea treaty the seabed past national zones cannot be taken by occupation or by planting a symbol. A country wanting more has to build a scientific case and submit it under the treaty process. Flag-planting does not enter into it. Russia followed that process with a revised submission in 2015 and two additions in 2021. On 6 February 2023 the UN commission agreed that the Lomonosov Ridge, the Mendeleev-Alpha Rise and the Podvodnikov Basin are natural extensions of Russia's shelf, while rejecting its evidence on the Gakkel Ridge. The commission does not decide who owns anything where claims overlap. Denmark filed for its part of the Arctic Ocean in 2013 and 2014 and Canada in 2019. Their claims overlap with Russia's near the Pole, the commission had not considered them as of 2023, and the overlaps have to be settled by negotiation. The flag, set there by a large state with an icebreaker, changed nothing about who owns what, and it remains a symbol.
arktika-2007-flag.why: Added what the treaty process actually produced: the February 2023 recommendations, and overlaps with Denmark and Canada. The Belfer piece dates from March 2023, so the 'not yet considered' status may have moved.

add_sources.t: Russia's Arctic Shelf Bid and the CLCS Explained, Belfer Center

arctic-sanctuary-greenpeace-flag.story:
The middle of the Arctic Ocean, around the North Pole, lies beyond the national zones of the five countries with Arctic coasts. No state rules those waters. The Arctic sanctuary is a proposal to protect that area from oil drilling and mining, promoted above all by the environmental group Greenpeace. It would work something like a nature reserve in international waters. As of 2016, only 4.7 percent of the Arctic marine area was protected.

Campaigners face a basic problem. A national government can create a park on its own territory by passing a law, but no single country has the power to do so for waters that belong to no country. There were also no international rules at the time for creating marine protected areas beyond national control, so an Arctic sanctuary would have needed new agreements between states. A treaty on marine life in areas outside any country's control, the BBNJ Agreement, took effect on 17 January 2026 and includes a procedure by which its parties can create protected areas on the high seas.

In April 2013 four young people working with Greenpeace, led by two young Indigenous people from the Arctic, trekked to the Pole. Their trip coincided with a meeting of the Arctic Council's senior officials at the Barneo ice camp, a temporary base on the sea ice. They cut a hole in the ice and lowered a flag designed by a child from Malaysia to the seabed about four kilometres down, at the spot where a Russian submarine had placed a flag in 2007. The flag was attached to a glass and titanium capsule holding the signatures of nearly three million people. Josefina Skerk, 26, a member of the Saami parliament in Sweden, said the area "belongs to no person or nation" and should be declared a global sanctuary, closed to oil companies and political posturing.

The flag was a piece of protest and made no claim. Its point was to answer the Russian flag with one standing for everyone. Neither flag had any legal effect on who may use the seabed.

Governments have taken up the idea in words. In 2008 the European Parliament raised the possibility of a treaty modelled on the Antarctic Treaty, and in a 2014 resolution it called for a sanctuary in the waters outside coastal states' zones. Such resolutions do not bind anyone. No sanctuary has been created, and it remains a campaign aim.
arctic-sanctuary-greenpeace-flag.why: Added the BBNJ Agreement, using the date and source already in the map's high-seas zone. The 'no rules at the time' sentence needed this.

add_sources.t: BBNJ Agreement, full text

svalbard-treaty.story:
Svalbard is a group of Arctic islands north of mainland Norway, about twice the size of Belgium. It has about 2,500 residents and no Indigenous people. It is often cited by people interested in places outside normal national rules, so it helps to know exactly how it works.

Until the 20th century Svalbard was terra nullius, land belonging to no state. Whalers came first and then miners from many countries, and they worked with almost no law. Once coal mining grew, disputes between miners and owners had no court to go to, and that created demand for someone to govern.

The answer was a treaty, signed in Paris on 9 February 1920 and in force from 14 August 1925. It recognises Norway's full and unqualified sovereignty, meaning supreme legal authority, over the islands. In exchange Norway accepted limits. Citizens and companies of every treaty country may live there and have equal rights to fish, hunt, mine and run businesses. Norway may collect only enough tax to pay for running Svalbard, so its budget is kept apart from the mainland's, and not all Norwegian law applies. Article 9 bans naval bases and fortifications, which restricts military use though the islands are not fully demilitarised. The whole archipelago is a visa-free zone under the treaty.

Russia uses its rights through its coal settlements at Barentsburg and Pyramiden. The treaty began with 14 parties and had 49 by 2026, the most recent being the United Arab Emirates in January 2026. Its reach is disputed. Norway reads the equal rights as covering only the islands and their territorial waters, and Russia says they cover the 200-mile fishery zone Norway set up in 1977 as well. Russia also rejects Norway's claim to exclusive rights over the continental shelf around Svalbard, and it disputes Norway's reading of Article 9, under which Norwegian armed forces may still go there to exercise sovereignty.

People sometimes describe Svalbard as a place belonging to no one where anyone can move. That is a misunderstanding. No visa is needed to enter, but Norway governs it, and a resident must obey Norwegian rules as they apply there. The treaty guarantees the right to come and do business, and it gives no right to rule anything.

The case shows the most workable form of unowned land being settled. Land with no government attracted people, the people's disputes created a demand for law, and the outside powers solved this by handing the land to one state on conditions. Nobody got an independent territory. A group wanting one today would find that the same process, if it happened, would most likely end with a government in charge.
svalbard-treaty.why: 49 parties confirmed. Added the live disputes over the treaty's reach from the listed source, since the story presented it as settled.

hawksbill-creek-freeport.story:
Freeport is a city on Grand Bahama island built under an agreement of 1955 between the government of the Bahamas and Wallace Groves. He received 50,000 acres, with an option on another 50,000, to create a city and free trade zone. The Grand Bahama Port Authority was formed to develop and administer the land, and it planned and built Freeport from nothing. It was exempted from taxes on income, capital gains, real estate and private property until 1985, and later changes extended the agreement to 2054.

The arrangement has lasted 71 years, through Bahamian independence, and its limits were tested in arbitration. The government claimed more than $357 million for 2018 to 2022, for customs, immigration, environmental oversight and regulation in the port area. The Authority counterclaimed for more than $1 billion and argued that it had exclusive authority over the area. A three-member tribunal chaired by Sir Anthony Smellie, with Lord Neuberger and Dame Elizabeth Gloster, issued a partial final award reported on 4 March 2026. It rejected the government's claim, because a 1990s review system, under which no new levels had been set, governs the payments. It rejected most of the counterclaims, including the argument for exclusive authority, and it found one breach over environmental bye-laws submitted in 2006, with no damages awarded so far. It confirmed that the government keeps its regulatory authority in Freeport and can use the review system to set the Authority's annual payments for future years, up to 2054. Both sides claimed victory. Past payments and costs remain unresolved.

This is a private company running a town under a state contract, enforced through arbitration and not through a treaty.
hawksbill-creek-freeport.why: Listed source checked; added the two things the tribunal confirmed, which are central to the entry.

sea-launch.story:
Sea Launch was a company founded in 1995 by four firms from Norway, Russia, Ukraine and the United States, with Boeing as manager. It launched satellites from the open ocean. Its rig, Odyssey, was a former floating oil-drilling platform that could move under its own power, and its ship, Sea Launch Commander, served as assembly plant and control centre. Rockets called Zenit-3SL were assembled in Long Beach, California, placed on the rig, and taken to the equatorial Pacific.

Launching at the equator gives a rocket extra speed from the Earth's spin. By 2014 the company had launched thirty-two rockets successfully, with three failures and one partial failure. The legal setup is why it matters. The company was registered in the Cayman Islands and its vessels were on Liberia's register, which the International Transport Workers' Federation criticised in 1997. Liberia has joined none of the four main space treaties.

An article in the Journal of Legal Research says that launching from the high seas, from a platform registered in a non-party, by a private consortium, made it hard to say which state was the launching state, and that the problem reached the UN's space committee. Governments reached the company anyway. Boeing paid $10 million in 1998 after US officials listed 207 export violations. US Customs tried to stop the rockets, classed as missiles, entering California.

Pacific island countries raised concerns at the UN in 1999 about fuel from discarded boosters. The company filed for bankruptcy in June 2009 and came out in October 2010 with Russia's Energia holding 95 percent. Its last launch was on 26 May 2014, S7 Group announced its purchase of the assets in September 2016, and the ships reached Russia's Slavyanka port in March 2020. China has launched more than a dozen missions from ocean platforms since 2019, and a US start-up called the Spaceport Company has a ship of its own, so the method has continued.
sea-launch.why: Dates tightened from the listed source; totals confirmed.

executive-outcomes.story:
Executive Outcomes was a private military company founded in South Africa in 1989 by Eeben Barlow, a former South African Defence Force officer, and Michael Mullen, as apartheid was ending and many soldiers were leaving. It recruited many former special forces men, and at its peak employed about 2,000 former soldiers. Clients were said to include large oil and mining companies and the governments of Angola, Sierra Leone and Indonesia. Several details of its history are disputed.

In Angola it trained and then fought for the government against UNITA, after UNITA rejected the 1992 election. Under pressure from the UN and the United States the government ended the contract. In Sierra Leone in March 1995 it contained the Revolutionary United Front insurgency and regained control of the diamond fields, and it forced a negotiated peace. The government then yielded to international pressure to have it withdraw. Later fighting took the rebels into the capital.

South Africa's Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act of 1998 prohibited direct participation as a combatant for private gain, and required official approval for military help abroad. The company gave input on the bill and is said to have been issued a licence, a point that is poorly documented. It was dissolved on 31 December 1998. In November 2020 Barlow stepped down from another security firm, STTEP, to restart the company, saying that some African governments had asked for it.

For anyone thinking of private force as a way to hold land, this is the most capable example, and its military contracts were for recognised governments. Even then its presence depended on foreign approval, and it had no claim to the land itself.
executive-outcomes.why: Licence claim is marked citation needed on the listed source; reworded. 2020 restart stated specifically.

asya-molvan-1948.story:
The Asya was a motor freighter owned by Naim Molvan, who was neither a citizen nor a resident of Palestine, then under British rule. On 27 March 1946 the British destroyer HMS Chequers sighted her on the high seas about 100 miles southwest of Jaffa. She was flying no flag. She later raised a Turkish flag, and when the boarding party came near she hauled it down and raised a Zionist flag.

She did not answer a signal asking where she was going. She had no passenger list and no normal ship's papers, and charts showed a course from France to a point near Tel Aviv. She was taken to Haifa with 733 people aboard, none with a passport or visa. The passengers were landed and sent to a clearance camp. The District Court of Haifa ordered the ship forfeited under the immigration law, and the Supreme Court of Palestine agreed.

The owner appealed to the Privy Council in London, then the final court for the British Empire, which ruled on 20 April 1948. He argued that the seizure happened on the open sea and broke international law. The court answered that freedom of the open sea is a freedom of ships that fly and are entitled to fly the flag of a state within the community of nations. The Asya met neither condition, so no question of international law could arise in its favour, and it "could not claim the protection of any State".

The case is still cited because the flag at issue was a flag of a people and a movement, with no state behind it at the time. It is the nearest old authority for what a self-made flag does at sea. The reasoning was given in a colonial immigration case before UNCLOS existed, and how far it reaches today is part of the current argument over stateless vessels.
asya-molvan-1948.why: Listed source checked, all facts match; added the judgment date.

perpetual-traveller-schultz-hill.story:
A perpetual traveller, sometimes shortened to PT, is a person who bases different parts of their life in different countries and avoids staying long enough in any of them to count as a legal resident. The stated aim is to reduce taxes and civic duties such as jury duty and military service, and to gain personal freedom.

The framing idea is flag theory. It is credited to the investment writer Harry D. Schultz, who proposed that everyone should have a second passport and an address in a tax haven, and that assets should be kept outside the home country. It was later expanded to five flags, adding a place where money is earned and a place where it is spent.

The idea was spread by Scope International Limited, a company in Waterlooville, England. It published books in the 1980s and 1990s under the name W.G. Hill, which may have been a pseudonym, and sold them through classified advertisements in The Times. One of them, published around 1989, was said to have been inspired and edited by Schultz, and a later handbook followed in 1993. Companies marketing offshore centres and tax schemes have used the idea as a staple.

It was never a place and it claimed no territory, so no state ever had to shut it down. The later spread of bank reporting and of residence-based tax tests changed what it can deliver. Who actually wrote the books is not firmly documented.
perpetual-traveller-schultz-hill.why: Removed research narration about Wikipedia per the style sheet. Facts not rechecked.

sealand-sale-attempts.story:
Sealand has been offered for sale more than once, and each episode shows what buying it could and could not bring. Sealand is a Second World War sea fort on two concrete legs, about 6 nautical miles off Suffolk, which the Bates family has called an independent principality since 1967. The first episode went badly for the family. In 1978 Alexander Achenbach, a German who described himself as Sealand's prime minister, invited Roy and Joan Bates to Austria to discuss a sale.

While they were away his hired men took over the fort. The Bates family retook it by helicopter and held Achenbach's lawyer for about six weeks. In January 2007 The Pirate Bay, a website that indexes file-sharing links, tried to buy Sealand after harsher copyright measures in Sweden pushed it to look for a base elsewhere. Between 2007 and 2010 Sealand was offered for sale through a Spanish estate company, InmoNaranja, at an asking price of €750 million, then about £600 million.

No sale was completed. The legal background made any sale an unusual one. Since 1 October 1987 the fort has stood inside Britain's 12-mile territorial sea. A court in Cologne held in 1978 that Sealand has no real territory, population or effective government, and no state recognises it. A buyer could at most have received possession of the structure and the family's claims. Britain's inaction so far has concerned one family doing little harm. It is reasonable to expect a different response to a file-sharing site accused of breaching copyright, though no court or government decided that, because the sale never happened.

HavenCo's experience on the same fort between 2000 and 2008 suggests the same limit, since a data-hosting firm that relied on the location for protection from courts could not keep customers or the site. Roy Bates died in 2012 and his son Michael took over, and the family continues to sell titles rather than the fort.
sealand-sale-attempts.why: Closing speculation reworded as reasoning. Facts not rechecked.

peanut-hole-okhotsk.story:
The Peanut Hole is a strip of international water in the middle of the Sea of Okhotsk, about 55 kilometres wide and 480 kilometres long. It lies more than 200 nautical miles from any coast, so it falls outside the exclusive economic zone of Russia, which surrounds it. That makes it high seas, open to ships of all countries, in the middle of a sea otherwise under one country's resource control.

Its name became known through fishing. Because any country could fish there, many did in 1991, and by 1992 they had taken perhaps as much as one million metric tons of pollock. Russia saw this as a threat, since the fish move between the pocket and its zone. In 1993 China, Japan, Poland, Russia and South Korea agreed to stop fishing there until stocks recovered, although they did not agree on what would follow.

The seabed then took a different path from the water. Russia argued to the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf that the sea floor there is part of its continental shelf. A subcommittee accepted this in November 2013, and in March 2014 the full commission agreed. Since then the seabed and subsoil have been treated as part of Russia's shelf, while the water remains high seas.

This shows how the law of the sea can split a place in two. A ship may sail there under its own flag as on any open ocean. Anything fixed to the bottom meets Article 80 of UNCLOS, which gives the coastal state control over artificial islands and certain structures on its shelf. A founder who saw an empty pocket of high seas on a map would find, on looking closer, that Russia holds exclusive rights over the seabed's resources and over structures fixed to it, and that the same state's zone surrounds the pocket on all sides.
peanut-hole-okhotsk.why: Shelf rights under UNCLOS are rights over resources and installations, not ownership. Wording corrected; source not refetched.
